utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I could be reminded, Mr. Whiting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you're probably aware, the B/C/S is on the English channel. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Maybe now they've switched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Do we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any protective measures? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Could the witness please say after me: I declare -- could somebody please interpret the witness to say after me, to take the declaration: I declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. I don't see the witness speaking. I'm not quite sure whether she's making the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think she didn't have the earphones on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: She didn't have the earphones, that's why. Okay. Let's start again. Will the witness please say after me: I declare that I will tell the truth ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe there's no connection. Let's have a connection and link with the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like her to say the following: I declare that I will tell the truth --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. The witness has taken the declaration --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Kesic.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Oh, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I begin, I'd like to, just as a matter of housekeeping, I'd like to give the -- this is a -- this witness is here for cross-examination only. I'd like to just give her 92 bis statement an exhibit number. It's in e-court, it's 01062734 and also 04656552. There are two parts to the 92 bis package, and if that -- if that could be -- that package -- those two parts could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May those two parts please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit 258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 258. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, also with the assistance of the usher I'd like to pass out to everybody a copy -- a hard copy of the witness's statement. I think it will be more convenient for the parties to refer to that rather than trying to see it on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mrs. Kesic, can you hear me and understand me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I hear you, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As you know, the -- your written statement which you signed and affirmed has been admitted into evidence, and so you will not have to answer -- I will not have to ask you to go through your story again because your written testimony is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I'm going to do, however, for everybody's benefit, so that we can follow your testimony, is I'm going to read a summary of your statement. So while I'm reading the summary, all you need to do is just listen - this is really for the benefit of us here in The Hague - and then when I'm finished reading the summary --

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When I'm finished reading the summary, I'll just ask you a few clarifying questions about your statement and then the Defence counsel will ask you some questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll read the summary now, and so all you need to do is just listen, please, until I start asking you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is just a summary of the statement. It's for the benefit of the Chamber and for the parties and also for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ana Kesic was born on the 21st of April, 1920, in Hrvatska Dubica, and she is a Croat. She has lived in Dubica all of her life, except from 1993 to 1995 when her village was occupied by SAO Krajina forces and she lived in Sisak. Again, for the convenience of the Chamber, Dubica, the village of Dubica can be found on page 21 of the atlas, Exhibit 23, at approximately D3 on the map. Relations between Serbs and Croats in Dubica were peaceful until 1990 to 1991. Sometime before September of 1991, the -- Serbs in Hrvatska Dubica left and went to Bosanska Dubica. Then in September of 1991, the Croats living in the village left, leaving only the elderly people. The witness believes that the Croats left because they did not have time to mobilise and resist the SAO Krajina forces, and so they left the village when they thought it was difficult to resist. On approximately 28 October 1991, three persons came to the witness's house: Velja Radunovic; Radovan Sosa, which is a nickname; and Janjeta, also a nickname. These men were driving a truck and asked the witness and the witness's sister-in-law, named Katarina, to attend a meeting. The witness believes that Velja was driving the truck and was in uniform, but she does not remember what uniform he was wearing. The witness and her sister-in-law got on the truck. Nine other people were picked up in neighbouring houses. Danica Krizmanic, Vera Stankovic, Pavle, Bara, Slavko Kucuk, Ruza Dikulic, Sofija Dikulic, and Nikola Loncar. All of the people in the truck were brought to the fire station in Dubica and were detained inside. After a few minutes, one of the guards in a green uniform came and asked for the witness, Mrs. -- no, I'm sorry, asked for Kesic. And the witness and her sister-in-law, Katarina, stepped forward and the guard told them to go home. As they were leaving, they saw a bus full of people arriving to the fire station. The people on the bus were from another part of the village of Dubica. Because it was raining, the witness could not see who the people were on the bus. When the witness and her sister-in-law returned home, they learned that some Serb neighbours from the Obrenovic family had sent someone to take them from the fire station. The witness says that she was released from the fire station because one of her relatives, Zdravko Vujic was then a 2nd lieutenant in the JNA navy in Split. Vujic is a Serb surname, and so they believed that he was a Serb and this is why the witness and her sister-in-law were released. The witness says that had they known her relative was a Croat, she would not have been released. After the witness returned to her house, she was told by a Serb neighbour that they should stay in the house, and this is what they did. The witness and her sister-in-law lived in the basement of the house. They could see Serb soldiers and policemen positioned on the hills and firing their weapons. The witness and her sister-in-law were afraid and could not sleep. They also saw Serb soldiers and policemen singing Krajina songs and they saw that they were drunk much of the time. One day the witness learned from a relative, Milan Sestic, that three of his neighbours had been killed: Batinovic, Luka Krnic, and Stef Uska. Later on, Milan Sestic disappeared and he has been missing since. The witness asked her Serb neighbours what happened to the missing Croats from the village and she was told that they had been sent to Knin and Glina to be exchanged. On the 3rd of August, 1993, the witness managed to leave Dubica and she went to Sisak. There she learned for the first time that all of the people who had been detained in the fire station in Dubica had been killed at Bacin. This was terrible news for the witness. After 1995, the witness returned to her village. Two mines were found in her house. Two houses on her street was completely burned down. A number of houses in other parts of the village were either burned down or damaged. Most of the houses had been looted and Serbs had taken away the valuables from them. The exhumation of the bodies in Bacin occurred in 1997. The witness attended the funeral for the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Kesic, I would just like to ask you a few questions about your statement to clarify just a few matters. In your statement you talked about some neighbours of Milan Sestic who were killed, a Batinovic, a Luka --

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A Luka Krnic and a Stef Uska. Were these people Serb or Croatian?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Croats, Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how about Milan Sestic; was he a Serb or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you returned from the fire station, you describe in your statement living in your house until 1993 when you left to go to Sisak. Could you describe for us how you felt --

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you describe for us how you felt during that time that you were living in your house from October of 1991 and 1993. How did you feel and what were the conditions?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, it wasn't exactly pleasant, but -- well, it was hard for us but it wasn't that there was anything lacking. We got aid from the Red Cross, you see, so we fared pretty well. We weren't hungry or something like that. As for the rest, we didn't go anywhere, we did nothing, we didn't have anything. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said in your statement that when you went to Sisak in 1993 you learned for the first time that the people detained in the fire station had been killed. Could you tell us briefly how it is that you learned that. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was told that when I went to say that I would live in Sisak. I went to report there that I had come from Dubica and that I would live with my niece in Sisak. Then she said to me -- well, I said that I came from Dubica and then she asked me -- she said: How come you managed to stay alive? Then I said to her: Well, they let us go, as you said, but -- I said to her then that -- well, I heard what you said, that there was this exchange. And then she said to me: What do you mean exchanged when they're all dead? They were all killed up there. Well, we call it the brook up there, the brook near Bacin, you know. They were all killed. And from Bosnia they saw them crying and shouting. That's the way it was. Then I felt so sick when she said that. That's where we had lived. Well, that's the way it was. Then this lady that wrote all of this down, this -- this registration that I would be living there in Sisak --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who -- Mrs. Kesic --

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Who -- who was this lady that you were speaking to?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was the lady that you were speaking to who told you this? Can you describe who she was, what position she had, what function?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, she was some kind of scribe. She wrote things down. She was a clerk. I reported there. She was writing things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why those people in the fire station were killed?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I cannot know that. I don't know that. I don't know that, why they did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were the people in -- who were killed in the fire station, do you know, were they Croats? Were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Only Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that when you returned to your house after 1995, there were houses that were looted and destroyed on your street and in other places in the village. Were these Serb houses or Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, they were Croat houses down there, Croat houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did -- did anything happen to the Catholic church in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Three were torn down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who tore them down?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat her answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mrs. Kesic, we couldn't hear your answer. Could you repeat it one more time. Who tore down the churches?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: The churches were torn down by the people who killed Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who were those people?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Now, who they were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were they Serbs or were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did anything happen to the Serb Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Nothing happened to it that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say "that time," are you referring to the time when you were in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think I do. Did something happen later to the Serb Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: No. It remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kesic. I don't have any further questions, and so now the Defence counsel will ask you questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic, the Bench -- the Chamber just wants to remind you that the cross-examination is limited to matters concerning Martic police or police and other SAO Krajina force in terms of the decision on the Prosecution's motion for the admission of written evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules of the 16th of January 2006. Of course the Defence is also allowed to ask questions arising from the questions that were asked by the Prosecution this afternoon in addition to the limitation in terms of that decision. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Kesic.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I am Predrag Milovancevic, attorney-at-law, Defence counsel for Milan Martic. I am going to put some questions to you concerning the matters that you spoke of in your statement. Can you hear me and understand me?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said that, apart from the period between 1993 and 1995, you spent your entire life in Hrvatska Dubica. Is that right, Mrs. Kesic?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I lived in Dubica, and then I went to Sisak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But otherwise did you spend your entire life in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, those three years, but then before that, yes, I lived in Dubica. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the relations between the Serbs and the Croats in Dubica were good until 1991, and then they worsened. I want to ask you whether Dubica was a mixed village, Croat and Serb?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Dubica was called Hrvatska Dubica, "Croatian Dubica."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why these relations between the Croats and the Serbs deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go anywhere, I didn't leave home. I don't know how this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor read your statement in which it says that at one point in time the Serbs left Dubica. Serbs who were the local population of Hrvatska Dubica left Dubica and then the Croats left as well. Do you remember when it was that the Serbs left Dubica?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Before this uprising, or whatever you call it. They left earlier. They went to Bosnia, you know, Bosanska Dubica. And I don't know why they were crossing over, why they went, whether they had something else on their minds. I don't know. I don't know why they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after the Serbs left and went to Bosanska Dubica, the population of Hrvatska Dubica who were Croats left in September. Who it was that left in September? I mean what was the age group of these people; younger people, older people, men, women, children or everybody?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Younger people left. Whoever had any transportation, they all left. Only we older people stayed behind. Only the elderly stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kesic.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time when the ethnic Croat population was leaving Dubica that the bridge was blown up. Do you know that? Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the Croat locals were leaving Dubica, was the bridge between Bosanska-Hrvatska Dubica blown up? Do you remember that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, there was peace on the bridge. They were guarding it, you know. Our Serbs were guarding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the bridge blown up? I'm asking you that. Was it destroyed at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Oh, it was destroyed, it was destroyed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the younger population left, whoever could leave.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Whoever could, left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Croats thought that they did not have enough time for mobilisation and resistance. What Croats; the Croats from the village or some Croats from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Please repeat what you said, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say to the Prosecutor that when the Croats left Dubica --

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- that it was believed that there is not enough time for mobilisation and that resistance could not be put up. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I didn't know about that, this resistance. There were just guards, Serb guards, whereas our Croats weren't there. They were guarding all of that, whereas the others left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of some three Serbs who were killed in Dubica; Stevo Djurcic, Petar Kojic and Stevo Vlatkovic?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I have not heard of that. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about whether among the population of Dubica, on the Croat and the Serb side - I'm referring to the population - do you know whether there were any armed people on both sides?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: The Croats were not armed; only the Serbs were armed. Not in Dubica, these people -- well, there was this police first but then when people were running away, they weren't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This police that you're mentioning in connection with running away, was that the Croat police in Dubica?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, there were those and others; half/half. Only the Croats left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kesic, in that period of time did you hear of the National Guards Corps, the so-called ZNG?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to move on to what happened in relation to the fire station. I have a few questions in that respect. In your statement you said that three persons came on the 28th of October, 1991, in a truck. They came and they were in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that they asked you and your sister-in-law to come to a meeting with them. Is that right, Mrs. Kesic?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could Mr. Milovancevic please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that these three men who came were Velja Radunovic, Radovan nicknamed Sosa, and some Janjeta?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the request is for you to speak a little slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you think that this Velja was driving the truck. Do you remember who it was that spoke to you out of these three men on that occasion? Who was it who asked you to come to the truck?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: This Janjeta, Janjeta, and this other one with him. I didn't know these people. Danica Krizmanic told me that. She said that this Janjeta was from the hill, and Radunovic, too. They said come to the meeting, and that was it. There was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kesic --

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- you said that you thought that this Velja was wearing a uniform. You mentioned some green uniform. Was this a military uniform or a forester's uniform or a third kind of uniform? You just described it as a green uniform. Do you recall that detail?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, greenish with these little things. I don't know whether it's military. I don't really know about these things. I don't know what kind it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On that morning, on that day, when they came to get you with the truck, was it raining? Do you remember that detail?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was raining, and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These people, these three men on the truck, did they perhaps have any kind of raincoats? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I think that they did not have any raincoats. And you know those caps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described that you and your sister-in-law complied with what these men said and that you boarded the truck and that you saw nine of your neighbours on the truck. Is that right, Mrs. Kesic?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And as one of your neighbours, you mentioned Slavko Kucuk as being one of your neighbours.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was he in the truck on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: He came up there with us by the Dom, but I didn't see him go. He was in front of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: There are people who say -- witnesses who say that that was on the 20th of October and not on the 28th of October, 1991. I'm thinking of October, the tenth month, 28th of October. Do you remember the exact date or are you giving us an approximation?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, it was October, yes. We call it "Listopad," the month of October. I don't know what you call it, but yes, the tenth month -- or rather, the eighth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution you said that several minutes after you arrived at the fire station that you and your sister-in-law were called out and that this was done by a guard wearing a green uniform and that he said that you could go. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes. He asked us -- he asked -- he said: Who's Kesic? And I said that that was me. And he said: Come over here. And then I called my sister-in-law over, and he said: The two of you can go home. You can go down there, and you'll go home, and that's how we went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement that after that you and your sister-in-law, Katarina, went home and that on the road beside you a bus passed by full of people and that it stopped in front of the fire station. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How far away from the fire station were you when the bus stopped in front of that fire station where you were before that?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, we were quite near our own street. We were entering our own street; quite a long way away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution you said that on the bus that passed by you the curtains were drawn and that it was raining and that --

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that that's why you couldn't see the people inside the bus. Is that right, Mrs. Kesic?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, then, how you can say that the bus was full of people from Donjani if you were not able to see who was inside the bus because of the rain and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see. No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- didn't the witness say in her statement they could not see who the people were? I thought when you put the question to her now and you summarised what you thought -- what you said she said, you said that she couldn't see the people inside. I think her statement said she couldn't see who the people; in other words, she couldn't identify and say that's so-and-so and that's so-and-so, but she could see that there were people inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the one but last paragraph of the B/C/S of her statement - and the last digits are 364 of that statement - she says that: "As the curtains were drawn on the windows of the bus and it was raining, we could not see who the people inside the bus were."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "... we could not see who the people inside the bus were." We were -- that statement says: I'm aware there are people inside, but who they are, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is why I asked her how does the witness know that they were people from Donjani? She saw some people but in continuation of her statement she's very specific and says that the people were from Donjani. So what I meant by asking my question was how she knew that these people were in fact from Donjani, if she could explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whether they were from Donjani. That makes it a different question completely. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kesic, so you were saying that this bus passed you by and you said that you couldn't distinguish the people inside because the curtains were drawn and it was raining. So how do you know, then, that they were people from Donjani? Did you see them then or did you hear about this later on? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, the place I mentioned, Donjani, is a little lower down, it's a little lower from our house. Because "donja" means lower down, so we call it Donjani, lower down. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kesic, can you explain to us how you knew that these were people from Donjani, the people in the bus? Did you know they were people from Donjani then, when the bus passed you by, or did you learn that later on? Do you understand what I'm asking you?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: The bus passed by and we could see that there were people inside, but we couldn't see which people were inside. But you could see that there were people inside, and the curtains were drawn and it was raining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the statement to the Prosecution you said that to you and Katarina, once you'd arrived home, your neighbours, the Obrenovic family - in fact, two women, Milka and Rosa, whose surnames you don't remember, so another two women - that they had sent Glisa Obrenovic to get you out of the fire station. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They said: We sent Glisa to get you out of there, to get you home, to get you back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived home, did this man Glisa come by later and tell you that you shouldn't leave your house or that you weren't to leave your house? And if he did say that, what did he think? How did he mean not to leave your house? In what sense?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what they said. They came and said don't go outside. Don't go out, and then nothing will happen to you. Just don't go outside, just don't leave your house, because there was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also say in your statement, mentioning your release, that they released you because a relative of yours was a lieutenant-colonel in the Yugoslav navy in Split and that they thought that he was a Serb and so that you were a Serb as well and that that's why they released you. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: His name -- his surname is Vujic. And there are a lot of Orthodox people with the surname Vujic in our village. So I -- I suppose they might have thought that that was it, and we were on good terms and that's the truth of it, so that's how that came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you something else. This guard wearing the green uniform who called your name out while you were at the fire station and who called out the name Kesic and then you two stepped forward, did he know you or did you know him? Did you know the man?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the man released you, did he mention this relative officer of yours in the Yugoslav navy?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So when you left the fire station, when you went outside, did you meet any other guards or did you happen to talk to anybody else about your 2nd lieutenant relative in the JNA navy?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: We didn't tell anybody else, no, but they knew about it. They knew who he was because we were all on very good terms. So they knew, on the basis of the name, the surname, that it was somebody who was Orthodox, judging by the surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you all this because of your statement which is linked to a conversation with that -- those neighbours of yours, the Obrenovics, and you said they sent Glisa to get us out. And then the conclusion you draw is that you were released because they thought, by mistake, that you were Serbs and not Croats, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Objection, objection, objection. The statement doesn't say that. What the statement says is that they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: She believes that they thought her relative was a Serb. It doesn't say anything about what they thought about her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't insist on that question. I'll withdraw it, not to make things more complicated with this witness, with your permission, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic, and while I'm at it, might I just remind you the limitations in terms of which your cross-examination is supposed to go. I have not yet picked up that you are asking on -- in terms of the motion that was granted. And I think you have gone far beyond the questions that were asked by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was questioning the witness only on matters that the Prosecutor asked her about -- or rather, he read out the statement. So those were the circumstances that I inquired about, and I thought that this was linked to Martic's police and everything else. So that's the context of it, and the witness experienced and lived through what she lived through and she's speaking about the context in which this happened. So I only have a few more questions and then I'll draw my cross-examination to a close. The witness is testifying about something that is very personal and the experience -- the terrible experience that she herself had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Kesic, I'm just going to ask you a few more questions. You said that you stayed there, in that place in 1993, until your sister-in-law, Katarina, died, and then you left and went to Sisak. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that Katarina died in July 1993 and that she was buried at the village cemetery. Can you tell us who buried Katarina? Who helped you with the funeral? Who helped you to bury her?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: A Serb helped me. He was the number one man in the municipality, and these foreign soldiers. And an officer ordered her body, which was in Kostajnica, to be brought to Dubica to our cemetery there. Yes, that's how it was, and that's how we buried her; our neighbours and us, we buried her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these neighbours of yours, were they Serbs? Were they the Obrenovic family that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. Yes, he's my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were they with you all the time, and how did they behave towards you?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, we were on very good terms. They were very good to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And finally, the Prosecutor asked you about the Catholic church in Dubica and who destroyed the church.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And he also asked you about the Orthodox church, and you said that on that occasion nothing happened to it, but when did something happen to it, then? When did something happen to the Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Not that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you live in Dubica in 1941 during World War II?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is that when the Orthodox church in Dubica was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, it was destroyed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. I apologise for having to take you back to these unfortunate and sad events, but that's our job. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mrs. Kesic, I have a few questions to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are there any villages around Dubica that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: A little louder, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are there any villages around Dubica that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know if anything happened in any one of those villages at around the same time as you were being called to the fire station?

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you. I wasn't there. Who came and who didn't come, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Kesic.

utterances.speaker: ANA KESIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the question from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Thank you very much. Mrs. Kesic, thank you once again very much for coming, and I -- may I repeat the statements that were made by counsel for the Defence: We are sorry to bring you back here and remind you of all these incidents that I would -- I think you would want to forget about. But as he says, it's our job we have to do and we thank you very much for coming. You are now excused, you may stand down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess you don't have any other witness for the day, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, we don't. And I apologise for the gap, it's just the necessity of the logistics here. So our next witness is not available until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Quite understandable, Mr. Whiting. Maybe we could use the last few minutes before the break to attend to housekeeping matters, if there are any. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The only matters that I'm -- well, there are two matters. The first is tomorrow's schedule. I understand that the morning, as it turns out, is not available and so there's been some discussion about -- to ensure that we finish the witness tomorrow, maybe taking slightly shorter breaks. I think that by doing that and possibly going over a few minutes, but maybe not even, we should have no difficulty finishing the witness tomorrow. I'll certainly try to go as quickly as I can with my direct examination and I'll try to take up less than half the time of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe so that there's a little bit of certainty in the minds of everybody around here, if you can venture an estimation of how long breaks we should take and by how many more minutes we might have to go beyond the time so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. I think that the -- if we took 20-minute breaks instead of half-hour breaks, that would be an advantage. And then I would not expect that we would have to go over more than half an hour, if that, and I don't even think that is likely to happen. It's very hard to estimate to the minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But that's the most -- that's the worst-case scenario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The worst-case scenario. If I may ask those who need the 30-minute break, would a 20-minute break tomorrow be reasonably okay for -- to do what has to be done during the breaks, the corrections on the translations and other things?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As far as the interpreters are concerned, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm not sure whether it is the interpreters only or there are technicians also involved in the work that is done during the break. Interpreter, are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can only speak for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay, I've just been told that there's no problem with that. Okay. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then the Chamber will expect your report in a week or so's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've just got an admonishment. We've got to make a redaction on this issue because of security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I wasn't aware of that. I didn't realise that there was a security issue involved there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. Obviously, then, we've come to the end of today's session. Court adjourned to tomorrow at 2.00 in the afternoon, same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of March, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.23 p.m.,
